Zambia has started connecting 751 health facilities across all 10 provinces with Starlink, and the first 90 kits went to Western Province. There's something poetic about where they started. Every year at the end of the rainy season the upper Zambezi floods the Barotse plain, and for centuries the Lozi king has left his compound at Lealui by royal barge and moved to higher ground at Limulunga. The ceremony is called Kuomboka. In Lozi it means "to get out of water." Now picture running fiber or building towers across land that turns into a lake for part of every year. A Starlink dish only needs a clear view of the sky, so the water below stops being the problem. In March 2020, months before Starlink had its first beta users, Elon Musk said it would serve the 3 or 4 percent hardest-to-reach customers, people with no connectivity or really bad connectivity. Six years later, with funding from the Global Fund through Zambia's Ministry of Health, clinics on one of Africa's great floodplains are being brought into the country's electronic health systems from orbit.

What's happening at Starbase, Texas is truly incredible. Deep in south Texas, Musk and his team have pulled in some of the most brilliant people on Earth to make space travel as normal and boring as air travel. The energy there is just insane. It feels like a modern day Manhattan project, but built for peace not war. The building pictured below is the actual factory where they build Starship, like a car factory for spaceships. You probably wouldn't have guessed it, since it looks like a nice office building. Most factories are cold and industrial but Starfactory feels warm, clean, with design touches that make you feel like you're in Silicon Valley. There's something really special happening here. I envy everyone who gets to work here and live here. Most people never get a chance to devote themselves to something so meaningful, something that potentially bends the river of human history. It kind of feels like a college town, except everyone's building spaceships instead of going to class.

BREAKING: SpaceXSI completes MiniHard construction in just ~5 months, with Gun Range targeting a ~4-month build. According to SemiAnalysis, SpaceXSI is roughly halving construction timelines while most comparable projects face 8–12 month builds. • MiniHard: Construction finished in approximately 5 months. • Gun Range: The new site just south of the Tennessee–Mississippi state line is targeting approximately 4 months of construction. • Colossus 1: Its first retrofit delivered 150 MW of capacity in 122 days. • Colossus 2: A subsequent retrofit delivered 210 MW in just 91 days. • Project SPAM: Work started October 5, with the first capacity targeted for December. • Massive expansion: SemiAnalysis projects the Memphis–Mississippi campus will grow from 0.4 GW of IT capacity in January to 2.4 GW by the end of 2026. That would be a sixfold increase in one year. • Five major projects: The expansion spans Macrohard, MiniHard, Macroharder, Project SPAM and Gun Range. • Tesla powering the scale: SemiAnalysis reports 1,377 Tesla Megapacks across Colossus 2, providing nearly 6 GWh of battery storage. The construction timelines and capacity forecasts are SemiAnalysis estimates, with future milestones still targets. Elon Musk’s teams are bringing extraordinary speed and scale to the infrastructure powering AI.

Nice paper on turning agent benchmarks into injection tasks. MetaPI takes an existing benchmark, finds plausible places to inject text, generates attack goals, optimizes adaptive payloads, and checks each attack in the real environment. They applied it to AppWorld, VitaBench, and Terminal-Bench. Closed models such as gpt-5.6-luna and claude-sonnet-5 were the most robust victims, but still had attack success rates above 20%. DataSentinel kept utility but reduced attacks less, while CaMeL reduced attacks at a large utility cost. If you already evaluate your agent on a utility benchmark, it's worth running injection attacks inside that same environment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10026 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/metapi-constructing-prompt-injection-benchmarks-from-llm-agent-benchmark-2611.10026

Interesting insights about agent memory. The bottom line is that you can't just rely on semantic relevance when picking memories. Most approaches pick the memory most similar to an agent's current state. But does that help it pick the next action? This work claims it often does not. Most retrieved memories have zero effect on the decision, and semantic relevance correlates poorly with usefulness. MemCredit measures each memory with controlled interventions, recording how the agent's action changes with and without it. A small estimator is trained on those credits. Relevance still collects the candidates, and the estimator decides which ones fit in the token budget. On ALFWorld with a 500-token memory budget, MemCredit reaches 86.57% success, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. It uses 152.1 memory tokens per decision, 74.5% fewer than BM25, and the agent policy is unchanged. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15600 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/memcredit-from-relevance-to-utility-for-decision-time-memory-in-long-horizon-web-2611.15600

Yes, the green flame is caused by burning copper from depleting fuel in the regenerative cooling circuit and going oxygen-rich (closer to stoichiometric temperature) in the main combustion chamber. Slight underperformance of engines on this flight is the reason. The booster is meant to land with tiny residuals, so the solution is to improve engine performance and performance consistency (underway with Raptor V3.2), as well as adjust flight software to do MECO1 about one second earlier to ensure enough propellant for boostback and landing (tiny change). These early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand, so this booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights.

I've been having several conversations with folks building in both spaces, and it's clear that without evals, that recursive self-improving loop is just more LOC without any clear value. You can't effectively automate what you cannot properly measure. Whatever product you use for agent automation should have a first-class way to measure and build evals explicitly, or support it easily. Pay close attention to this. And this isn't just about software engineering/coding; it's across all functions of the org.

a few days ago we published the "No AI Slop Manifesto" at @aiDotEngineer Code Summit in SF, written in collaboration with many of the speakers and attendees It already hit the front page of hacker news, has 300+ signatures including folks from Baseten, SpaceX, OpenAI, PostHog, Shopify, Glean, ZoomInfo, and legendary builders including @swyx @poteto @kentcdodds @mihail_eric @audreyt @altryne @traviscline @philipkiely @TejasKumar_ read and sign it at slopmanifesto dot com some of my favorite points > AI cannot replace human judgement, it can only amplify our judgement (or lack thereof). > We own the intent, taste, and consequences of what we ship, however much AI helps us make it. > There will always be alpha in reviewing *something*. As models improve, we may stop reading most of the code. We may still review a plan, design, or result, because if we don't, we just get the same output as everyone else.

The traffic from agent swarms doing research is going to be quite large, they are relentless. I had Fable 5.2 reconstruct WH Auden's 1941 poetry class. It found an obscure, relevant book on the Internet Archive, which it read a line at a time by doing repeated full text searches.

But we also don't want to stop agents from doing relevant academic research (or even commercial research, since it might mention your product) with too many gates and barriers. In any case, I donated to the Internet Archive for my use of the commons, but better solutions needed.
